name: Ine of Wessex
title: King of Wessex
roles: Patron of Glastonbury and the see of Sherborne
summary: King of Wessex from 688 to 726 whose law code is the earliest to survive from any English kingdom outside Kent, and who abdicated in 726 to travel to Rome.
details: Ine held Wessex for thirty-seven years, fought Dumnonia, Sussex, Kent and Mercia, and issued the law code that is the main evidence for how early West Saxon society was organised — including the British population living under West Saxon rule. He abdicated in 726 and died at Rome.
overview: Ine ruled the West Saxons for some thirty-seven years, from 688 to 726, and matters above all for the code of laws he issued in the 690s. It is the earliest West Saxon law to survive and the first written by any English king outside Kent, and it shows a kingdom in which British and Saxon inhabitants lived side by side under one law that valued them differently.

His reign also pushed Wessex west into Dumnonia, east against the South Saxons and north against Mercia, secured a settlement with Kent over the killing of Cædwalla’s brother Mul, and endowed the church at Glastonbury and the new see at Sherborne. In 726 he gave up the kingdom and went to Rome, where he died; the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle and Bede agree on the abdication, and everything after it is later tradition.
greatestFeats: Issued the earliest surviving West Saxon law code, in the 690s
Settled with Kent in 694 over the killing of Mul
Pushed the West Saxon frontier into Dumnonia and fortified Taunton
Endowed Glastonbury and supported the new bishopric at Sherborne

birth.note: Son of Cenred, a West Saxon of royal descent who was still active during his son’s reign; no birth date or place is recorded. His sister Cuthburh founded the minster at Wimborne.

death.circumstance: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle says he went to Rome after abdicating in 726 and died there; no date, burial place or account of his death survives.

quickFacts.knownFor: The earliest surviving West Saxon law code

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Ine ruled the West Saxons for some thirty-seven years, from 688 to 726, and matters above all for the code of laws he issued in the 690s. It is the earliest West Saxon law to survive and the first written by any English king outside Kent, and it shows a kingdom in which British and Saxon inhabitants lived side by side under one law that valued them differently.

His reign also pushed Wessex west into Dumnonia, east against the South Saxons and north against Mercia, secured a settlement with Kent over the killing of Cædwalla’s brother Mul, and endowed the church at Glastonbury and the new see at Sherborne. In 726 he gave up the kingdom and went to Rome, where he died; the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle and Bede agree on the abdication, and everything after it is later tradition.

contentSections.title: Birth and early life
paragraphs: Nothing is recorded of Ine before he became king. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle names his father as Cenred and traces the descent back to Cerdic through Ceawlin, as it does for every West Saxon king it recognises; his sister Cuthburh married a Northumbrian king, left him, and founded the double minster at Wimborne. Cenred was still issuing land and appears in the prologue to his son’s laws, so Wessex in these years may have been ruled by father and son together rather than by a single king.

He came to the throne in 688 when Cædwalla, who had conquered Sussex, the Isle of Wight, Surrey and Kent in a violent three-year reign, abdicated and set out for Rome to be baptised. Cædwalla died there in April 689, ten days after his baptism, leaving Ine an overextended supremacy and a feud with Kent.

contentSections.title: Character and Personality
paragraphs: Ine left no chronicler of his own and no hagiographer, so what can be said about him comes from what he did rather than from what anyone wrote about him. The laws are the nearest thing to a personal record, and they read as the work of a ruler concerned with order and with revenue: baptism within thirty days of birth, church dues rendered by Martinmas, the man who leaves the highway without shouting or blowing a horn treated as a thief, and fines for fighting in the king’s house that rise with the rank of the offender.

Bede, writing within a decade of his death, describes him warmly and briefly, and says only that after thirty-seven years he handed the kingdom to younger men and went to Rome to spend his last days near the shrines of the apostles. That is the earliest statement of the story, and it frames the abdication as piety rather than defeat. The Chronicle preserves a harder set of facts alongside it — a long sequence of campaigns, an exile killed after three years of pursuit, and a queen who razed one of her husband’s own strongholds so it could not be held against him.

Later tradition made much more of him than the sources support. Glastonbury claimed him as a founder and produced charters in his name; William of Malmesbury in the twelfth century gave him a pious queen, Æthelburg, who persuaded him to renounce the world; and the story of the Schola Saxonum, the English quarter in Rome, was attached to him by Roger of Wendover in the thirteenth. Modern historians such as Barbara Yorke and Frank Stenton set those aside and describe what the code and the annals will carry: a durable, methodical king whose long reign gave Wessex the institutions it fought the ninth century with.

contentSections.title: The law code
paragraphs: Ine issued his laws with the counsel of his father Cenred, Bishop Hædde of Winchester, Bishop Eorcenwald of London and his ealdormen and councillors. The code cannot be dated exactly and belongs somewhere between 688 and 694; it is the earliest surviving law from any English kingdom outside Kent and the foundation document of West Saxon government.

It survives by an accident of editing. Nearly two centuries later Alfred the Great appended Ine’s code to his own domboc rather than superseding it, and it is preserved with Alfred’s laws in the manuscript now at Corpus Christi College, Cambridge. That means the text we read passed through a ninth-century compilation, and scholars are careful about how much of the arrangement, and possibly the wording, is Alfred’s work rather than Ine’s.

The contents are practical and unsentimental: wergilds and the compensations owed for injury and theft, the obligations of lords for their dependants, penalties for harbouring fugitives, the duties owed from an estate in food rents, provisions on grazing, fencing and woodland, and the church dues that make it the first English law to treat the church as a taxing institution rather than only as a beneficiary.

contentSections.title: Britons and Saxons under one law
paragraphs: The most quoted feature of the code is its treatment of the wealh, the British inhabitants of the lands Wessex had absorbed. They appear not as outsiders but as a graded part of the population, with their own landholders, riders and slaves — and with wergilds set at roughly half those of English people of the same standing. A Briton holding one hide of land is valued at 120 shillings where the English ceorl stands at 200; a Briton with five hides reaches 600; the king’s Welsh horseman, a man in royal service, is set at 200.

That arithmetic is the clearest evidence there is for how conquest actually worked in seventh-century Britain. The British population of Somerset, Dorset and Devon was not exterminated or wholly displaced: it was absorbed into a legal order that recognised its property and its status while pricing its lives lower. The code also assumes British slaves alongside English ones, and mixed households, and it needs rules for both.

The vocabulary of rank in the code — the gesith, the lord’s man holding land and answerable for his followers, and the ceorl, the free farmer — is the earliest full picture of early English social structure, and much of what is said about seventh-century society in any modern account ultimately rests on these clauses.

contentSections.title: Wars, Dumnonia and the frontier
paragraphs: Ine’s first achievement was to end the Kentish feud. In 694 the people of Kent came to terms and paid him thirty thousand — the Chronicle’s figure, in a unit it does not specify — in compensation for having burned Cædwalla’s brother Mul and twelve men with him in 687.

The long war was westward, against the British kingdom of Dumnonia in what is now Devon and Cornwall. In 710 Ine and Nothhelm of the South Saxons fought Geraint, king of the Britons, and the West Saxon frontier moved to the Tamar over the following generation. Around 710 Ine had a fortress built at Taunton to hold the new ground, which is the first appearance of the town in the record.

The reign’s later years were spent on rivals closer to home. He fought Ceolred of Mercia in 715 at Woden’s Barrow on the Wiltshire downs, with no recorded result. In 722 his queen Æthelburg razed Taunton, which an ætheling named Ealdberht had taken and held against him; Ealdberht fled into Surrey and Sussex, and Ine invaded the South Saxons twice to hunt him, killing him in 725.

contentSections.title: The church in Ine’s Wessex
paragraphs: When Bishop Hædde died in about 705 the West Saxon see was divided, and Aldhelm — abbot of Malmesbury, the most accomplished Latin writer in England of his generation — became the first bishop of Sherborne for the lands west of Selwood. The division was a working response to a kingdom that had grown and to a frontier whose British Christians had their own practice; Aldhelm had already written to Geraint of Dumnonia urging the British clergy to adopt the Roman Easter.

Ine endowed Glastonbury, in the marshland his family controlled, and its later community remembered him as a founder and preserved charters in his name of doubtful authenticity. He is also credited with the first church at Wells in 705, on the site of the cathedral, where a floor stone still marks his reign. The laws give the endowments their institutional counterpart: church-scot is owed from every free household at Martinmas, and the penalty for withholding it is heavy.

contentSections.title: Abdication and Rome
paragraphs: In 726, after thirty-seven years, Ine gave up the kingdom. Bede says he handed it over to younger men and went to Rome to end his days near the shrines of the apostles; the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle adds that his wife Æthelburg went with him. The pilgrimage followed a pattern already set in his own family circle — Cædwalla had gone to Rome to be baptised and died there in 689, and Cenred of Mercia and Offa of Essex had gone the same way in 709.

What happened afterwards is not recorded. No date of death, no burial place and no account of his last years survive, and the later claim that he founded the Schola Saxonum, the English quarter and hostel by St Peter’s, first appears in a thirteenth-century chronicle and is also told of Offa of Mercia. William of Malmesbury’s story that Æthelburg persuaded him to abdicate by showing him a hall stripped bare after a feast is a good tale from four centuries later.

He left no son. The kingdom went to Æthelheard, whom one late source calls his brother-in-law, and whose accession was contested by an ætheling named Oswald; the Chronicle notes that Æthelheard held the kingdom fourteen years and that Wessex was already feeling Mercian pressure. The succession dispute is the clearest sign that the long stability of Ine’s reign was personal rather than structural.

contentSections.title: Legacy
paragraphs: Ine’s code outlived his dynasty’s memory of him because Alfred the Great chose to keep it. By attaching it to his own laws rather than replacing them, Alfred made Ine’s clauses part of the working law of a much larger kingdom, and preserved for later readers the only detailed view of West Saxon society two centuries before the Danish wars.

The territorial gains lasted as well. The push into Dumnonia and the fortification of Taunton set the line from which Egbert of Wessex completed the conquest of Cornwall in the ninth century, and the shire structure of Somerset and Devon grew in ground Ine’s reign secured. A king with no battle that anyone remembers is, by way of a legal text and a frontier, one of the more consequential rulers of pre-Viking England.

keyAchievements.title: The earliest West Saxon laws
keyAchievements.description: A code issued in the 690s with Cenred, Bishop Hædde and Bishop Eorcenwald, preserved because Alfred the Great appended it to his own.

keyAchievements.title: Settlement with Kent
keyAchievements.description: In 694 the Kentish people paid thirty thousand in compensation for burning Cædwalla’s brother Mul, closing a dangerous feud.

keyAchievements.title: The western frontier
keyAchievements.description: Campaigns against Geraint of Dumnonia from 710 and the fortress at Taunton pushed West Saxon power towards the Tamar.

keyAchievements.title: Church building
keyAchievements.description: Endowed Glastonbury, supported the new see of Sherborne under Aldhelm, and is credited with the first church at Wells.

timeline.title: Becomes king of Wessex
timeline.description: Succeeded Cædwalla, who abdicated to be baptised at Rome and died there in April 689.

timeline.title: Issues his law code
timeline.description: Promulgated with his father Cenred, Bishop Hædde of Winchester and Bishop Eorcenwald of London; the earliest English law outside Kent.

timeline.title: Settles with Kent
timeline.description: Accepted thirty thousand from the Kentish people as compensation for the burning of Cædwalla’s brother Mul in 687.

timeline.title: Sherborne and Wells
timeline.description: The West Saxon see was divided on Hædde’s death and Aldhelm became bishop of Sherborne; Wells remembers Ine as founder of its first church.

timeline.title: Campaign against Dumnonia
timeline.description: Fought Geraint, king of the Britons, alongside Nothhelm of the South Saxons, opening the westward advance.

timeline.title: Taunton fortified
timeline.description: Built a stronghold to hold the new ground in Somerset; its first appearance in the record.

timeline.title: Meets Ceolred of Mercia
timeline.description: Fought the Mercian king at Woden’s Barrow on the Wiltshire downs; the Chronicle records no outcome.

timeline.title: Æthelburg razes Taunton
timeline.description: His queen destroyed the fortress after the ætheling Ealdberht seized it, denying a rival the stronghold.

timeline.title: Kills Ealdberht
timeline.description: Invaded the South Saxons for the second time and killed the exiled ætheling who had taken refuge with them.

timeline.title: Abdicates and leaves for Rome
timeline.description: Gave the kingdom to Æthelheard and travelled to Rome with Æthelburg; Bede says he went to end his days near the apostles’ shrines.

predecessor.note: His predecessor, who conquered Sussex, Kent and the Isle of Wight, then abdicated in 688 to be baptised at Rome, where he died in April 689.

successor.note: King of Wessex from 726 to 740, called Ine’s brother-in-law by one late source; his accession was contested by an ætheling named Oswald.
